metadata.methods_description: Participants performed a virtual-town courier task followed by free recall of delivered items. Read-only sessions generated training data for classifiers. In closed-loop sessions, classifiers predicted recall success and stimulus presentation was timed to coincide with predicted good or poor memory encoding.

citation_details.title: Causal and Chronological Relationships Predict Memory Organization for Nonlinear Narratives
citation_details.author: James W. Antony, Angelo Lozano, Pahul Dhoat, Janice Chen, Kelly A. Bennion
citation_details.abstract: While recounting an experience, one can employ multiple strategies to transition from one part to the next. For instance, if the event was learned out of linear order, one can recall events according to the time they were learned (temporal), similar events (semantic), events occurring nearby in time (chronological), or events produced by the current event (causal). To disentangle the importance of these factors, we had participants watch the nonlinear narrative, Memento, under different task instructions and presentation orders. For each scene of the film, we also separately computed semantic and causal networks. We then contrasted the evidence for temporal, semantic, chronological, or causal strategies during recall. Critically, there was stronger evidence for the causal and chronological strategies than semantic or temporal strategies. citation_details.title: Decoding EEG for optimizing naturalistic memory
citation_details.author: Joseph H. Rudoler, James P Bruska, Woohyeuk Chang, Matthew R. Dougherty, Brandon S Katerman, David J. Halpern, Nicholas B. Diamond, Michael J. Kahana
citation_details.abstract: Background Spectral features of human electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings during learning predict subsequent recall variability. New method Capitalizing on these fluctuating neural features, we develop a non-invasive closed-loop (NICL) system for real-time optimization of human learning. Participants play a virtual navigation and memory game; recording multi-session data across days allowed us to build participant-specific classification models of recall success. In subsequent closed-loop sessions, our platform manipulated the timing of memory encoding, selectively presenting items during periods of predicted good or poor memory function based on EEG features decoded in real time. Results We observed greater memory modulation (difference between recall rates when presenting items during predicted good vs. poor learning periods) for participants with higher out-of-sample classification accuracy. citation_details.title: Brain Networks and Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Alzheimer’s Disease: From Mechanistic Insights to Clinical Applications
citation_details.author: Jie Ma, Juanjuan Lu, Qi-Hao Guo, Xu‐Yun Hua, Jian‐Guang Xu
citation_details.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a continuously progressing clinical and biological spectrum, in which synaptic dysfunction and the resulting brain network abnormalities serve as core mechanisms underlying the transition from subjective cognitive decline (SCD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia. This chapter is organized into three sections. The first section provides an overview of brain network alterations across the different stages of AD, including both resting-state and task-related networks. The second section introduces methods for assessing brain network function, such as multimodal neuroimaging and EEG. The third section focuses on non-invasive brain stimulation techniques for AD, including transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), which aim to restore cognitive function by modulating brain network activity.

citation_details.title: Specialized recall procedures
citation_details.author: Lynn J. Lohnas, Sean Matthew Polyn, Michael J. Kahana
citation_details.abstract: Studies of memory search using the free recall paradigm have advanced our understanding of human memory for more than a century. Here, we review seven specialized recall procedures that depart from methodological orthodoxy: the inter-list repetition procedure, the list-before-last procedure, the recall-by-category procedure, the final-free recall procedure, the overt-rehearsal procedure, the externalized recall procedure, and the spatial-temporal recall procedure. Key empirical findings from each of these procedures have challenged existing theories and led to theoretical advances.

citation_details.title: Spectral Correlates of Encoding Distinguish Good from Poor Learners
citation_details.author: Ben Falkenburg, A. Broitman, M. Kahana
citation_details.abstract: Individuals vary in their ability to encode and recall new experiences, yet neural markers of memory have rarely been linked to these trait-level differences. Subsequent memory effects (SMEs) identify patterns of neural activity during encoding that predict whether an item will later be remembered or forgotten. In scalp EEG, SMEs are typically characterized by increased theta and gamma power with decreased alpha, a profile that has been interpreted as a signature of effective encoding. Here, we tested whether SMEs reflect individual differences in mnemonic ability by analyzing over 1.3 million encoding events from a large free recall dataset. citation_details.title: What masking geometry works best for EEG foundation models?
citation_details.author: Pierre Guetschel, Bruno Aristimunha, Yassine El Ouahidi, Arnaud Delorme A, Thomas Moreau, Michael Tangermann
citation_details.abstract: EEG foundation models hold promise for scalable brain-signal decoding across clinical and cognitive neuroscience applications, yet their pre-training pipelines remain poorly understood. Among design choices, the masking strategy is particularly critical: it determines what the network must predict and from which context. Yet it has never been ablated in isolation, as each new model bundles a new masking strategy with a new backbone and objective. In this paper, we formalize the design choices for spatio-temporal masking strategies and train various models with a single pipeline under varying masking configurations across two SSL frameworks (MAE and JEPA). We then systematically evaluate the resulting 58 pre-trained models on the 12 datasets of OpenEEGBench under a linear probe. Both frameworks agree on an optimal masking configuration and on shared failure modes. Outside these, performance is robust: 11 MAE and 9 JEPA configurations are statistically indistinguishable from the best. We further identify a novel JEPA-specific failure mode, tagged bias-inflation collapse, invisible to standard detectors. With a well-chosen mask, our pipeline reaches REVE-level downstream performance at a fraction of REVE's pre-training compute.

citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai C
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.
